metadata.scope: e_persia (all baronies across k_khorasan, k_daylam, k_makran, and k_kabulistan)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if unattested or not established in available sources).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 CE start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 CE (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 CE exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_ardabil.first_mention_attestation: Attributed to Sasanian king Peroz I (r. 459–484 CE) in Islamic historiography; attested in 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri) and in the 8th-century CE Armenian history of Lewond as Artavet.
b_ardabil.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Iranian/Avestan *arta- (sacred law/order) and *vēt- (willow), reflected in 8th-century CE Armenian Artavēt (per Vladimir Minorsky).

b_khalkhal.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by Yaqut al-Hamawi in 1220 CE (617 AH) as a town and district (kura) adjacent to Gilan.

morphemes.translation: obscure / possibly connected to ancient Kharkhar

b_khalkhal.etymology_analysis: Vladimir Minorsky suggested a possible connection to the Neo-Assyrian toponym Kharkhar in the eastern Zagros, though the town itself is unattested before 1220 CE.

b_unar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Onar in Hamdallah Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub (1340 CE), which ascribes its earlier foundation as Shadar/Shad Firuz to Peroz I.
b_unar.etymology_analysis: Toponym of a village in Meshgin Shahr County, Ardabil; unattested in written sources prior to the 14th century CE.

b_sarat.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sarat (Serat) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) as a stage on the road from Ardabil to Zanjan.
b_sarat.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic itinerary stage between Ardabil and Zanjan, often identified with Sarab (Arabicized or manuscript variant Sarat).

b_bailaqan.first_mention_attestation: Reportedly founded by Sasanian king Kavad I (r. 488–531 CE) and surrendered to Arab commander Salman ibn Rabiah c. 645 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan).
b_bailaqan.etymology_analysis: Middle Iranian *Bel-akan, connected by Vladimir Minorsky to Baylaman in Gilan, reflecting Sasanian-era Caspian resettlement in Arran.

b_barza.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Barza in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) among the cities of Adurbadagan.
b_barza.etymology_analysis: Iranian toponym (cognate with *barz- 'high'), attested in 9th-century CE Arabic geographical lists for Adurbadagan.

b_darband-qarabuli.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_darband-qarabuli.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Persian-Turkic compound ('pass of Qarabuli'); unattested in historical sources by 867 CE.

b_basawa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Yaqut al-Hamawi (early 13th century CE) and Hamdallah Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub (1340 CE) as Basava/Pasava.
b_basawa.etymology_analysis: Vladimir Minorsky derived the medieval name Basava/Pasveh from ancient Parsua via r-deletion in consonant clusters, though the form Basava is first attested in the 13th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Neo-Assyrian annals (9th century BCE), linked to Pasveh/Basava by Vladimir Minorsky
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Iron Age polity in the Lake Urmia basin whose name survived in Pasveh.

b_maragha.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Maraghah during the stay of Umayyad prince Marwan ibn Muhammad c. 740 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan).

morphemes.translation: Arabicized: place where an animal rolls, folk etymology of local name

b_maragha.etymology_analysis: Explained by Arab chroniclers as 'place where animals roll' (due to cavalry dung in 740 CE), though Vladimir Minorsky considered it an Arabic folk etymology of a pre-existing local name.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical accounts of Mark Antony's 36 BCE Parthian campaign (Phraaspa/Phraata); al-Baladhuri (Akra-rudh)
older_name_by_867.notes: Winter capital of Atropatene identified with Maragha.

b_kursara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kulsarah (Kul-sera) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) as a market town 10 farsakhs from Maragha.
b_kursara.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement in Adurbadagan between Khunaj and Maragha, recorded as Kulsarah in 9th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_leylan.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name as Leylan in Hamdallah Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub (c. 1340 CE) as a town under Maragha.
b_leylan.etymology_analysis: Modern town in the Miandoab plain near the ancient ruins of Ganzak; the name Leylan itself is unattested before the 14th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical and Sasanian sources (capital of Media Atropatene, identified near Leylan)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Achaemenid and Atropatene capital situated near modern Leylan.

b_khunaj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Khunaj in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) as a city 7 farsakhs from Miyaneh on the road to Maragha.
b_khunaj.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic town in southeastern Azerbaijan (later deformed to Khuna and renamed Kaghazkonan by the 13th century CE).

b_ar-ran.first_mention_attestation: Middle Persian Arran / Arabic al-Ran (ar-Ran), attested in 6th-century CE Syriac/Middle Persian sources and 7th–9th-century CE Arab conquest narratives (al-Baladhuri).
b_ar-ran.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (al-Ran) of Middle Persian Arran, the Iranian choronym for Caucasian Albania and later the Kura-Aras lowland.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical sources (Strabo, 1st century BCE) and Armenian sources
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greek/Latin and Armenian names for the region of Arran.

b_shiz.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Shiz in early Islamic conquest accounts (651 CE surrender of Ardabil) and in Ibn Khordadbeh (9th century CE) as the site of the great Zoroastrian fire temple.
b_shiz.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic name for the fortified sanctuary at Takht-e Soleyman, housing the Sasanian royal fire temple of Adur Gushnasp.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Sasanian Middle Persian sources and 4th-century CE Peutinger Map
older_name_by_867.notes: Sasanian fire temple name for the Shiz sanctuary.

b_tabriz.first_mention_attestation: Rebuilt by Zubaydah in 791 CE and attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (9th century CE) as al-Tawrezh; earlier attested in Middle Persian/Armenian as T'awrezh/T'avrezh.
b_tabriz.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Persian tap-riz ('flowing hot', referring to thermal springs) or linked to Proto-Iranian/Assyrian Tarui-Tarmakisa.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Assyrian King Sargon II's epigraph of 714 BCE
older_name_by_867.notes: Iron Age fortress name equated with Tabriz in modern scholarship.

b_marand.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Maranda/Mandagarana in Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE) and as Marand in Ibn Khordadbeh (9th century CE).
b_marand.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement in northwestern Iran attested since the 2nd century CE (folk-etymologized in Armenian tradition as 'mother lies here').

b_dihnakhirjan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Deh-Nakhirjan in Yaqut al-Hamawi (early 13th century CE), who derived it from Nakhirjan, treasurer of Khosrow II.
b_dihnakhirjan.eponym_details: Traditional etymology in Yaqut al-Hamawi derives the name from Nakhirjan, treasurer of Sasanian King Khosrow II (r. 590–628 CE).
b_dihnakhirjan.etymology_analysis: Persian compound 'village of Nakhirjan'; later known as Dehkhwaraqan and renamed Azarshahr in the 20th century CE.

b_ujan.first_mention_attestation: Old city of Ojan (Ujan), first mentioned in historical chronicles from the 6th century AH (12th century CE), later serving as an Ilkhanid summer capital.
b_ujan.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the site of modern Bostanabad, attested from the 12th century CE onward.

b_ahar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (Ibn Hawqal referring to 334 AH / 945–946 CE; Hudud al-Alam, 982 CE).
b_ahar.etymology_analysis: Town in Qaradagh/Arasbaran; while pre-Islamic ruins exist nearby, the name Ahar is first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic/Persian geographies.

b_dizmar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by Hamdallah Mustawfi in Nuzhat al-Qulub (c. 1340 CE) as a district north of Tabriz.
b_dizmar.etymology_analysis: Toponym containing Iranian *diz ('fortress'), first attested in the 14th century CE despite Sasanian-era ruins in the district.

b_talish.first_mention_attestation: First attested as T'alish in the 5th-century CE Armenian translation of the Alexander Romance.
b_talish.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym for the southwestern Caspian coast and mountains, named after the indigenous Talysh people.

b_aparshahr.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Abarshahr in Shapur I's 262 CE inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, as well as on Sasanian coins and clay sealings.
b_aparshahr.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian *Aparn-xšahr ('land of the Aparni', per Josef Marquart); historically a Sasanian province in Khorasan (Nishapur), placed in Talish in the game.

b_urmiya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Urmia in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) as a major city of Adurbadagan.
b_urmiya.etymology_analysis: Debated between Urartian origin (Richard Frye), Indo-Iranian *urmi- 'wave' (T. Burrow), and Syriac Ur-Mia 'city of water' near Lake Urmia.

b_ushnuya.first_mention_attestation: First described by 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal) as a fair-sized town attached to Urmia.
b_ushnuya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Islamic town (modern Oshnavieh) on the route from the Urmia basin to Rawandiz; first attested in 10th-century CE geographies.

b_salmas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Salmas in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE) among the cities of Adurbadagan.
b_salmas.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement northwest of Lake Urmia (with Sasanian rock reliefs nearby), attested in 9th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_gher.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_gher.etymology_analysis: No documented historical settlement named Gher is attested in the Urmia region by 867 CE.

b_daylam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 6th-century CE Byzantine sources (Procopius as Dolomitae) and Syriac records (Daylomaye; Church of the East diocese c. 790 CE).
b_daylam.etymology_analysis: Mountainous highland region of inland Gilan named after its inhabitants, the Daylamites.

b_gilan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gelae in classical Greco-Roman sources (Strabo, Pliny, 1st century BCE–1st century CE), as Gelan in Shapur I's 262 CE inscription, and as a Nestorian bishopric in 553 CE.
b_gilan.etymology_analysis: Iranian choronym meaning 'land of the Gilites (Gelae)', attested since classical antiquity (repository placeholder Landolfstat is an intra-county disambiguation).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Landolfstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Landolf
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_lahij.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Lafjan (Lahijan) in the Persian geography Hudud al-Alam (982 CE).
b_lahij.eponym_details: Legendary tradition attributes its foundation to Lahij ibn Sam ibn Nuh, a mythical/biblical figure not attested in early Arabic geographies.
b_lahij.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Lafjan in 982 CE; unattested in written sources prior to the late 10th century CE.

b_qazvin.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Sasanian king Shapur I (r. 240–270 CE), refounded by Shapur II (r. 309–379 CE), and conquered by Arab forces under al-Bara' ibn Azib in 644 CE.
b_qazvin.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form of Middle Persian *Kaspin/Kazwin, likely connected to the ancient Caspii people.

b_alamut.first_mention_attestation: Fortress constructed c. 840 CE (some sources cite 860 CE) by the Justanid ruler of Daylam, Wahsudan ibn Marzuban.
b_alamut.etymology_analysis: Daylami compound meaning 'eagle's teaching' (or 'nest of punishment'), referring to the legend of an eagle indicating the crag to Wahsudan ibn Marzuban.

b_abhar.first_mention_attestation: Conquered in 643 or 645 CE by al-Bara' ibn Azib during the Arab conquest of Iran (al-Baladhuri).
b_abhar.etymology_analysis: Persian compound 'water-mill' (locally pronounced Awhar), referring to the water mills powered by the Abhar Rud.

b_zanjan.first_mention_attestation: Conquered in 645 CE by al-Bara' ibn Azib (al-Baladhuri); earlier attested in Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE) as Aganzana.
b_zanjan.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form of Persian Zangan, related to classical Aganzana.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE) for Aganzana; Hamdallah Mustawfi attributing Shahin to Ardashir I (r. 224–242 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical and early Sasanian names for Zanjan.

b_afshar.first_mention_attestation: Oghuz Turkic tribe first attested as Awshar in Mahmud al-Kashgari's Diwan Lughat al-Turk (1072–1074 CE), entering Iran during the Seljuk era.
b_afshar.eponym_details: Legendary eponym Afshar, son of Yildiz Khan and grandson of Oghuz Khan (recorded by Rashid al-Din Hamadani, 14th century CE).
b_afshar.etymology_analysis: Oghuz Turkic ethnonym (glossed as 'obedient' or 'swift/active' in medieval sources), unattested in northwestern Iran before the 11th century CE.

b_suhravard.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE, Ibn Hawqal c. 977 CE) as a town in Jibal.
b_suhravard.eponym_details: Derived from the pre-Islamic Iranian personal name Sohrab (Suxrap-kart / Suhrav-gerd), per Theodor Nöldeke and Josef Marquart.
b_suhravard.etymology_analysis: Iranian compound from personal name Sohrab + -gerd/-vard ('town of Sohrab'), first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_kerend.first_mention_attestation: Modern village and city (Korand/Kerend) in Dashli Borun District, Gonbad-e Kavus County, Golestan Province, Iran; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in eastern Golestan (etymology uncertain)

b_kerend.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement name in the Turkmen Sahra plain of eastern Golestan (distinct from Kerend-e Gharb in Kermanshah).

b_dihistan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dihistān in early Islamic histories (al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri) during Yazid ibn al-Muhallab's 716–717 CE campaign against the Sul/Chol Turks; named after the Dahae confederacy attested in Strabo (1st century BCE).
b_dihistan.eponym_details: Named after the ancient Dahae (Old Iranian *Dāha-) nomadic confederacy.
b_dihistan.etymology_analysis: Persian Dihistān ('land of the Dahae'), preserving the ethnonym of the ancient Dahae confederacy.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Liutbrandstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Liutbrand
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_khodzhakala.first_mention_attestation: Modern village (Hojagala/Khodzhakala) in western Turkmenistan near the Sumbar valley and Kopet Dag; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_khodzhakala.etymology_analysis: Turkmen compound Khodzha-kala ('fortress of the khwaja/master'), reflecting post-Islamic Perso-Arabic-Turkmen toponymy.

b_oboy.first_mention_attestation: Village (Oboý) in Bereket District, Balkan Province, Turkmenistan, established in 1840 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_oboy.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkmen settlement name in the Kyurendag foothills, founded in the 19th century CE.

b_gurgan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Old Persian Varkāna in Darius I's Behistun Inscription (522 BCE) and Greek Hyrcania; Middle Persian Gurgān and Arabic Jorjān, refounded as a Muslim city by Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in 716–717 CE.
b_gurgan.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Varkāna ('land of wolves'), rendered in Greek as Hyrcania, Middle Persian as Gurgān, and Arabic as Jorjān.

b_astarabad.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE); later tradition attributes its founding to Yazid ibn al-Muhallab (716–717 CE) on a village called Astarak, but pre-867 existence is uncertain.

morphemes.translation: star (or mule, folk etymology; or village Astarak)

b_astarabad.etymology_analysis: Persian Astarābād (Esterābād), connected by medieval tradition with a village Astarak or Persian setāra ('star') + -ābād.

b_bakrabad.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE) as the industrial left-bank suburb of Gorgan (Jorjān) across the Gorgan River; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bakrabad.eponym_details: Compound with personal name Bakr + -ābād ('settled/built by Bakr'); specific historical eponym unattested.
b_bakrabad.etymology_analysis: Perso-Arabic compound Bakrābād ('settlement of Bakr'), the silk-manufacturing quarter of medieval Jorjān.

b_abaskun.first_mention_attestation: First securely dated in the 909–910 CE Rus' raid (Ibn Isfandiyar), with an earlier undated raid during the reign of Hasan ibn Zayd (864–884 CE); no contemporary written attestation strictly <= 867 CE.
b_abaskun.etymology_analysis: Medieval Caspian port name likely derived from the local river Sokanda (attested in Ptolemy's Geographia, 2nd century CE).

b_ganja.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 859–860 CE by Arab governor Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Yazid ibn Mazyad according to the Tarikh Bab al-Abwab (with a later tradition in Mustawfi placing it in 659–660 CE).
b_ganja.etymology_analysis: From Persian ganj ('treasure'), traditionally explained by a treasure unearthed during the city's foundation.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_mingachevir.first_mention_attestation: Modern city founded in 1948 CE; although archaeological excavations revealed ancient settlements and a 4th–7th century CE Caucasian Albanian church complex, the name Mingachevir has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_mingachevir.etymology_analysis: Modern Azerbaijani city name established in 1948 CE at the Kura River crossing; folk etymologies connect it with a river crossing or personal name.

b_barda.first_mention_attestation: Built under Sasanian King Peroz I (r. 459–484 CE) as Perozabad, attested as Partaw (485–488 CE) in Movses Kaghankatvatsi, fortified by Kavad I as Perozkavad, and became seat of the Albanian Catholicos in 552 CE.
b_barda.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bardha'a (modern Barda) derives from Old Armenian Partaw, either from Iranian *pari-tāva- ('rampart') or *Parθaυ ('Parthian').

b_paytakaran.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the city of Paytakaran in 4th-century CE events in Faustus of Byzantium, as well as in Sebeos (7th century CE) and the Ashkharhatsoyts (7th century CE).
b_paytakaran.etymology_analysis: Armenian P'aytakaran, interpreted by Anahit Perikhanian as 'land of P'ayt' from Median *karan- ('border, region').

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica (c. 20 CE); Shapur I Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription (c. 260 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Roman Caspiane (c. 20 CE) and Sasanian Balasagan (c. 260 CE) designated the overlapping lower Kura-Araxes territory.

b_gabarawan.first_mention_attestation: Listed as Ghabrawan among the cities of Adurbadagan by the 9th-century Persian geographer Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, first compiled c. 846 CE).

morphemes.translation: settlement name in early Islamic Adurbadagan

b_gabarawan.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic Iranian toponym attested in Ibn Khordadbeh's list of Adurbadagan towns.

b_varsan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Warthān/Varsān in al-Baladhuri's account of Umayyad governor Marwan ibn Muhammad's administration (c. 732–744 CE) and in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) as the northernmost town of Adurbadagan.

morphemes.translation: border town on the Araxes (often linked to Vardanakert)

b_varsan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Warthān (Persian Vartān / Azerbaijani Varsan), widely identified in historical geography with Armenian Vardanakert.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Anania Shirakatsi, Ashkharhatsoyts (7th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Identified by S. Yeremyan and others with Armenian Vardanakert attested in the 7th-century Ashkharhatsoyts.

b_langarkanan.first_mention_attestation: Modern Lankaran (earlier Langarkunān/Langarkanān); establishment date is unknown and historical records begin in the late medieval/early modern period, with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: place of dropping/weighing (or Talysh lankran 'cane house')

b_langarkanan.etymology_analysis: Persian Langarkunān/Langarkanān ('place for dropping/weighing anchor', i.e. seaport), or from Talysh lankran ('cane house').

b_nakorzan.first_mention_attestation: Medieval town in Kovsakan (Syunik) near the Araxes and Hakari confluence; attested in later Armenian historiography without a verified written attestation strictly <= 867 CE.
b_nakorzan.etymology_analysis: Armenian toponym Nakorzan (Nakork'an) for a town at the northern end of the Khoda Afarin bridge on the Araxes.

b_barzand.first_mention_attestation: Attested in al-Tabari as the fortified military base of Abbasid general al-Afshin in 835–837 CE (220–222 AH) during the campaign against Babak Khorramdin, and listed by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

morphemes.translation: town name in eastern Adurbadagan / Mugan

b_barzand.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic Iranian town name in Mugan/Adurbadagan, a key fortified station on the Ardabil–Warthan road.

b_shemakha.first_mention_attestation: 743–744 CE (construction of the Juma Mosque of Shamakhi; served as capital of the Shirvanshahs from the 8th century CE, succeeding classical Kamachia recorded by Ptolemy c. 150 CE).
b_shemakha.etymology_analysis: Modern Shamakhi (Şamaxı / Šamāḵī) continues the ancient toponym Kamachia recorded by Ptolemy.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (2nd century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Attested as Kamachia in Ptolemy's Geographia before becoming medieval Shamakhi.

b_kabala.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder as Cabalaca, capital of Caucasian Albania (Naturalis Historia 6.29, 77 CE), Ptolemy as Khabala (2nd century CE), and Anania Shirakatsi as Kavalak (7th century CE).
b_kabala.etymology_analysis: Derives from ancient Caucasian Albanian Kabala (Pliny's Cabalaca, Ptolemy's Khabala, Armenian Kapalak/Kavalak).

b_kudevan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found in historical or encyclopedic sources.
b_kudevan.etymology_analysis: Toponym of uncertain origin in the Shaki/Shirvan region without pre-867 CE attestation.

b_paidangaran.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Syriac Church of the East records (Synodicon Orientale): Bishop Yohannan of Paidangaran (first mentioned 540 CE, adhered to the Synod of Mar Aba I in 544 CE) and Bishop Ya'qob (554 CE).

morphemes.translation: Syriac ecclesiastical form corresponding to Paytakaran/Baylaqan

b_paidangaran.etymology_analysis: Syriac rendering of the regional toponym in the 6th-century Church of the East synodal acts.

b_baku.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly attested in writing as Bākūh/Bākūya in 10th-century CE Arabic geographers (al-Mas'udi, c. 943 CE; al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE), though Roman inscriptions (84–96 CE) survive nearby at Gobustan.

morphemes.translation: God (proposed Bagavan) or later folk etymology bād-kūbe ('wind-pounded')

b_baku.etymology_analysis: Early Arabic Bākūh/Bākūya, often derived from Old Iranian *Bagavān ('place of God'), with a 19th-century folk etymology from Persian bād-kūbe ('wind-pounded').

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_maras.first_mention_attestation: Corresponds to Maraza (modern Gobustan) in Mountainous Shirvan, Azerbaijan; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_maras.etymology_analysis: Local Shirvan toponym (Maraza, renamed Gobustan in 2009 CE), lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_shirvan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in al-Baladhuri's account of the first Arab incursion into the eastern Caucasus (before 650 CE), when the Shirvanshah submitted to Salman ibn Rabi'a al-Bahili (with Ibn Khordadbeh attributing the title to Sasanian king Ardashir I, r. 224–242 CE).

morphemes.translation: historical region name (possibly from Shahrbān 'governor' or Caspian Iranian)

b_shirvan.etymology_analysis: Iranian regional name Sharwān/Shīrwān, possibly derived from Middle Persian shahrbān ('governor/satrap').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Schirwân — Disambiguated capital seat from sub-barony Bakû
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_salyan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 13th-century CE Mongol invasion era (called Dalan-Navur in Mongolian); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_salyan.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Arabo-Persian seyl/seylan ('flood, overflow') or Turkic sal ('raft').

b_firrim.first_mention_attestation: Became the residential stronghold of the Bavandid dynasty in the eastern mountains of Tabaristan under Surkhab I in the late 7th century CE (c. 665 CE) and is attested in early Islamic histories of Tabaristan.

morphemes.translation: Bavandid mountain stronghold in eastern Tabaristan

b_firrim.etymology_analysis: Tabari/Persian toponym Ferīm/Firrim, seat of the early Kayusiyya branch of the Bavandids.

b_larijan.first_mention_attestation: Mountainous district along the Lar River in Tabaristan/Mazandaran; attested in medieval Islamic sources from the early 10th century CE (e.g., homeland of Asfar ibn Shiruya, fl. 913 CE), with no verified written attestation strictly <= 867 CE.
b_larijan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Lar River (Lār) in the Alborz mountains with the Iranian regional suffix -ījān.

b_uram.first_mention_attestation: Historical center of the Fadusban/Paduspan mountain district east of Sari in Tabaristan; attested in 12th–15th century CE Islamic sources (e.g., Ibn Isfandiyar), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: mountain settlement name in eastern Tabaristan

b_uram.etymology_analysis: Medieval Tabaristani toponym (Ūram / Uram-khast), administrative center of the Paduspan highland district.

b_amul.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Sasanian mint signature 'AM' from Bahram V (r. 420–438 CE), as a Syriac diocese in 554 CE (Bishop Surin of 'Amol and Gilan'), and as Abbasid capital of Tabaristan from 760 CE; named after the ancient Amardi tribe.
b_amul.eponym_details: Named after the ancient Amardi (Mardi / Amui) tribe of the southern Caspian coast.
b_amul.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the ancient Amardi (Pahlavi Amui) people who inhabited the region.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_tamisha.first_mention_attestation: Garrisoned by Abbasid governor Abu al-Abbas al-Tusi in 763 CE and prominent in al-Tabari's account of Mazyar's revolt in 839 CE; Sasanian Tammisha Wall and Bansaran Fort date to the 5th–6th centuries CE.
b_tamisha.etymology_analysis: Persian Tamīšah/Tamīša, the eastern border town of Tabaristan guarding the coastal corridor toward Gorgan.

b_sariya.first_mention_attestation: Reconstructed/founded under Dabuyid ruler Farrukhan the Great (r. 712–728 CE), who named it Saruyeh/Sariya after his son Saruya and made it capital of Tabaristan.
b_sariya.eponym_details: Named after Saruya (Saruyeh), son of the Dabuyid ispahbadh Farrukhan the Great (r. 712–728 CE).
b_sariya.etymology_analysis: Named Sarūya (Arabicized Sāriya, modern Sārī) after Saruya, son of Farrukhan the Great.

b_ruyan.first_mention_attestation: First appears in historical records in the Letter of Tansar (under Ardashir I, r. 224–242 CE) as part of king Gushnasp's realm; granted to Baduspan I in 665 CE and conquered by Abbasid forces in 761 CE.

morphemes.translation: reddish mountain (proposed identification with Avestan Raodita)

b_ruyan.etymology_analysis: Western Tabaristan highland district; James Darmesteter connected Rūyān with Avestan Raodita ('reddish' mountain) and Bundahishn Royishnomand.

b_natil.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Nātil/Nātilah, a major Abbasid-era city and military garrison in western Tabaristan (8th–9th centuries CE), corroborated by 9th–12th century CE archaeological finds.
b_natil.etymology_analysis: Medieval Tabari toponym Nātil (modern Natal) in the Ruyan/Nur plain.

b_shalush.first_mention_attestation: Captured by Abbasid forces under Umar ibn al-Ala in 761 CE during the Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan and garrisoned in 763 CE as a frontier town facing Daylam.
b_shalush.etymology_analysis: Persian/Tabari Chālūs, rendered in early Arabic sources as Shālūs or Sālūs.

b_bamian.first_mention_attestation: Attested by the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian (c. 400 CE) and in detail by Xuanzang (c. 630 CE, as Fan-yen-na), as well as in the 8th-century travelogue of Hyecho (727 CE) and early Abbasid accounts (al-Ya'qubi).
b_bamian.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle Persian Bāmīkān ('shining/brilliant place'), reflecting the valley's prominence as a Buddhist sanctuary and Silk Road hub.

b_sakalkand.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographical works: the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, as Sakalkand) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, as Iskalkand), and later in al-Biruni's Canon (c. 1030 CE).
b_sakalkand.etymology_analysis: A Hindu Kush/Tukharistan settlement name ending in the Eastern Iranian urban element -kand ('town, settlement').

b_parwan.first_mention_attestation: The town of Parwan (Farwan) is first clearly attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers, notably the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, spelt Barvan, 'Gate of Hindustan') and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, as Farwan).
b_parwan.etymology_analysis: Persian/Eastern Iranian toponym Parwān (Arabicized Farwān), a key pass town north of Kabul leading over the Hindu Kush.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Alexander historians (Arrian, Strabo, Pliny) for Alexandria in the Caucasus (329 BCE) and Xuanzang (644 CE) for Kapisa (Kai-pi-shi)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Kapisa / Alexandria in the Caucasus (modern Bagram) served as the pre-Islamic urban center of the Parwan basin prior to the attestation of Parwan.

b_panjhir.first_mention_attestation: First attested on Saffarid silver dirhams of Ya'qub ibn al-Layth minted at al-Banjhir in AH 259 (872–873 CE) following his 870 CE campaign, and subsequently in 10th-century Islamic geographers (Ibn Hawqal 977 CE, Hudud al-'Alam 982 CE).
b_panjhir.etymology_analysis: Medieval sources (Ibn Battuta 1333 CE; Le Strange) explain Panj-hīr (Arabicized Banjhīr) as 'Five Hills/Mountains'; the modern form Panjshīr ('Five Lions') is a later folk-etymological reinterpretation.

b_jarbaya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographical works: the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, as Jāriyāna, spelt Khāriyāna) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, as Jārbāya) as a silver-mining town near Panjhir.
b_jarbaya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Hindu Kush mining settlement attested in Arabic and Persian geographies as Jārbāya or Jāriyāna.

b_chitral.first_mention_attestation: The name Chitral is attested only in early modern chronicles and 1764 CE Manchu annals; medieval Chinese and Islamic sources up to the 16th–17th centuries refer to the region as Bolor (Balur) or part of Uddiyana.
b_chitral.etymology_analysis: Derived from Khowar ćhitrār ('field'), ultimately from Sanskrit kṣetra ('field, land').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Faxian (c. 400 CE) for Uddiyana and 5th-century CE Chinese records (later 9th-century Arab Balad-i Bolur) for Bolor
older_name_by_867.notes: Before the attestation of Chitral, the mountain region was known in Chinese and Islamic sources as Bolor (Balur) or part of Uddiyana.

b_kunar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in Babur's Baburnama (early 16th century CE, c. 1519 CE); earlier archaeological remains at Chaga Serai date to 800–1000 CE without written attestation of the name Kunar.
b_kunar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kunar River (the lower course of the Chitral River), a major tributary of the Kabul River.

b_kabul.first_mention_attestation: Recorded by Ptolemy in his Geography (c. 150 CE) as Kaboura (Καβουρα), in Chinese Han/Later Han annals as Gaofu, by Xuanzang (644 CE), and in early Islamic conquest accounts from 664–665 CE as Kābul.
b_kabul.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient hydronym of the Kabul River, attested in Rigvedic Sanskrit as Kubhā and in Classical Greek as Kophen/Kophes.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Rigveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) as Kubhā; Classical Greek authors (Strabo, Arrian) as Kophen/Kophes
older_name_by_867.notes: The Rigvedic hydronym Kubhā and Greek Kophen designated the Kabul River and its basin prior to Ptolemy's Kaboura (150 CE).

b_sukawand.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Islamic accounts of the Saffarid sack of its Hindu/Zhun temple by Fardaghan under Amr ibn al-Layth in 896–897 CE, and later in al-Istakhri (951 CE), Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE), and al-Biruni (c. 1030 CE).
b_sukawand.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic Sakāwand/Sukāwand (modern Sajawand in Logar), a major pre-Islamic pilgrimage site; scholars have linked the first element to Sanskrit Sukhāvatī or the Saka ethnonym with the Iranian suffix -wand.

b_lamghan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Aramaic inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka at Laghman (c. 260 BCE), in the Mahāmāyūrī Tantra (1st–3rd c. CE) as Lampāka, in Ptolemy (2nd c. CE) as Lambagae, and by Xuanzang (7th c. CE) as Lan-p'o (Lampaka).
b_lamghan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Lamghān (modern Laghmān) is the Persian/Arabic evolution of ancient Sanskrit/Prakrit Lampāka.

b_nagarahara.first_mention_attestation: Recorded by Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) as Nagara, also called Dionysopolis, by Faxian (c. 400 CE) as Na-kie, and by Xuanzang (c. 630 CE) as Na-ka-lo-ho (Nagarahāra).
b_nagarahara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Nagarahāra ('city-district'), an ancient Buddhist center near modern Jalalabad, later contracted to Ningnahar/Nangarhar.

b_ghazna.first_mention_attestation: Possibly mentioned by Ptolemy (VI.18.4, c. 150 CE) as Gázaca/Gāzaca, and attested by Xuanzang (644 CE) as Ho-si-na/Jaguda as well as in early Islamic conquest accounts of Zabulistan from the 7th–8th centuries CE.
b_ghazna.etymology_analysis: Derived from Iranian *ganja-/*gazna- ('treasury, storehouse'), reflecting its role as a commercial entrepôt on the route to India.

b_gardiz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Gardizi's Zayn al-akhbar for the year 256 AH (870 CE), when its local ruler Abu Mansur Aflah ibn Muhammad Khaqan was attacked by the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, and later in the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE).
b_gardiz.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian/Persian compound ending in -diz ('fortress, citadel'), describing the fortified mound town between Ghazni and Kurram.

b_istakh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographical works: al-Istakhri (951 CE, p. 280), the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.21 as Istākh), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, pp. 296, 349) on the road between Ghazni and Bamiyan.
b_istakh.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement (variously spelt Istākh/Astākh/Asnākh) located two stages north of Ghazni toward Bamiyan.

b_sharan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in ancient or medieval written sources; modern provincial capital of Paktika Province, Afghanistan.
b_sharan.etymology_analysis: Modern Pashto toponym (Sharan/Sharana) with no documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_moqor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in ancient or medieval written sources prior to 867 CE; modern town and district center in southwestern Ghazni Province.
b_moqor.etymology_analysis: Modern Afghan toponym along the Ghazni–Kandahar road, possibly reflecting Arabic muqarr ('halting-place') or a local tribal/place name.

b_rukhaj.first_mention_attestation: Arabic al-Rukhkhaj is attested in early Islamic conquest accounts of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura (653–654 CE) and Rabi ibn Ziyad (671 CE) in al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari.
b_rukhaj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized from Middle Persian *Raxwaθ / Old Persian Harauvatiš ('rich in waters', cognate with Sanskrit Sarasvatī), originally a hydronym for the Arghandab basin.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Behistun Inscription of Darius I (520 BCE) as Harauvatiš; Classical Greek authors as Arachosia
older_name_by_867.notes: Arabic al-Rukhkhaj continues Achaemenid Old Persian Harauvatiš and Hellenistic Arachosia.

b_rudan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as R.zān in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (c. 869 CE, p. 396) and as Rūdhān in al-Istakhri (951 CE, p. 248) and the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.17), a salt-producing borough near Rukhkhaj.
b_rudan.etymology_analysis: Persian Rūdhān ('rivers/streams'), denoting a settlement situated on streams in the Rukhkhaj region.

b_panjway.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Gardizi's Zayn al-akhbar for Ya'qub ibn al-Layth's 870 CE campaign through Bust and Panjway, and as Banjaway (capital of al-Rukhkhaj) in al-Istakhri (951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (977 CE), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE).
b_panjway.etymology_analysis: Iranian Panj-wāy (Arabicized Banjaway), meaning 'Five Streams', referring to the confluence of streams near modern Panjwayi west of Kandahar.

b_bakrawath.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bakrāwādh (for Bakrābād) in al-Muqaddasi (985 CE), while al-Istakhri (951 CE) and Ibn Hawqal (977 CE) give the form Takīnābādh (also mentioned by Gardizi for Ya'qub's 870 CE campaign).
b_bakrawath.eponym_details: Bakrābād ('Bakr's settlement') incorporates the Arabic personal name Bakr; the variant/earlier name Takīnābādh incorporates the Turkic title/name Tegin (Takīn).
b_bakrawath.etymology_analysis: Persianized compound Bakrābād (Arabicized Bakrāwādh), 'settlement of Bakr', lying one stage from Banjaway on the Sibi road.

b_qandahar.first_mention_attestation: Arabic Qandahār is attested in accounts of Umayyad governor Abbad ibn Ziyad's campaign (673–681 CE) and Hisham ibn Amr al-Taghlibi under al-Mansur (754–775 CE) in al-Baladhuri, as well as in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).
b_qandahar.eponym_details: Often linked in tradition to Iskandar (Alexander the Great, 356–323 BCE), who founded Alexandria in Arachosia on the site in 330 BCE; modern scholarship also connects the name to Gandhara.
b_qandahar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Qandahār/Kandahār, either derived from the ancient Indo-Iranian regional name Gandhāra or from a contraction of Iskandariya (Alexandria).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek and Roman sources (c. 330 BCE) and Ashoka's bilingual Greek-Aramaic edict at Old Kandahar (c. 260 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE as Alexandria in Arachosia on the foundations of an earlier Achaemenid fortress.

b_jaldak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in ancient or medieval written sources prior to 867 CE; attested in modern Afghan history and geography as a district in Zabul Province.
b_jaldak.etymology_analysis: Modern Afghan toponym (Tarnak wa Jaldak district in Zabul Province) with no documented pre-867 attestation.

b_mapan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in ancient or medieval written sources prior to 867 CE; modern locality in Zabul Province, Afghanistan.
b_mapan.etymology_analysis: Modern locality name in Zabul Province with no documented medieval or ancient written attestation.

b_zamindawar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in al-Baladhuri's account of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura's 653–654 CE expedition to the shrine of Zun in Zamindawar, and in 769 CE under Ma'n ibn Za'ida.
b_zamindawar.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Zamīn-i Dātbar ('Land of the Justice-Giver'), referring to the pre-Islamic deity Zun worshipped there.

b_sarwan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers: al-Istakhri (951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (977 CE), and the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.11 as Sarvān/Sharwān) in the Bust/Zamindawar region.
b_sarwan.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in Zamindawar/Bust attested in 10th-century Islamic geographies as Sarwān or Sharwān.

b_bishang.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers: al-Istakhri (951 CE, p. 244, as Bishlank) and the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.14, as Bishlang) on the frontier of Zamindawar and Ghur.
b_bishang.etymology_analysis: Medieval district and tribal name (Bishlank/Bishlang) on the Zamindawar–Ghur frontier.

b_durgas.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers: al-Istakhri (951 CE) and the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.12, as Durghush/Darghash), a frontier fort of Zamindawar against Ghur on the Helmand River.
b_durgas.etymology_analysis: Medieval frontier fortress in Zamindawar along the upper Helmand, attested as Darghash/Durghush in 10th-century sources.

b_bagnin.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers: al-Istakhri (951 CE, p. 244, as Baghnīn) and the Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, § 24.13, as Baghnī), a town near Ghur one march west of Dartall.
b_bagnin.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the Zamindawar–Ghur frontier (Baghnīn/Baghnī), corresponding to modern Baghran/Baghni.

b_balkh.first_mention_attestation: 520 BCE Behistun Inscription of Darius I (as Old Persian Bāxtriš) and Avestan Vendidad (as Bāxδī); later Classical Greek Bactra (Herodotus, Strabo, Arrian).

morphemes.translation: Bactria / Bactra (etymology debated; possibly Old Iranian *bāxtri-)

b_balkh.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Iranian *Bāxtri- / Avestan Bāxδī (Old Persian Bāxtriš, Greek Bactra), evolving through Middle Iranian into New Persian/Arabic Balkh.

b_ribat-i-el-kif.first_mention_attestation: c. 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, p. 291, as Ribat Dhi'l-Kifl, a fortified river-crossing station on the Oxus opposite Ribat Dhi'l-Qarnayn on the Balkh–Tirmidh/Bukhara route). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ribat-i-el-kif.eponym_details: Named after the Quranic prophet Dhu'l-Kifl (Quran 21:85, 38:48, traditionally identified with Ezekiel), whose shrine/ribat stood at the Oxus crossing.
b_ribat-i-el-kif.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Ribāṭ Dhi'l-Kifl ('ribat of Dhu'l-Kifl'), a river-crossing guard-station on the Oxus near Tirmidh/Balkh attested in 10th-century CE geography.

b_shapurqan.first_mention_attestation: 891 CE (al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan, p. 287, as Shaburkan, noting an earlier local principality there); later 10th-century CE geographers (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, Hudud al-'Alam). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_shapurqan.eponym_details: Attributed to Sasanian king Shapur I (r. 240–270 CE) or Shapur II (r. 309–379 CE): Middle Persian Šāpūr-gān ('city/place of Shapur').
b_shapurqan.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Šāpūrgān ('city of Shapur'), Arabicized as Šubūrqān / Ušbūrqān (modern Sheberghan); while the nearby Tillya Tepe burials date to the 1st century CE, the written toponym is first attested in late 9th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_navida.first_mention_attestation: c. 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, p. 291, as Nawida, a small town with a congregational mosque at an Oxus crossing used by travelers from Samarqand). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_navida.etymology_analysis: Recorded by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Nawīda, a river-crossing settlement on the Oxus in the Balkh–Transoxiana borderlands.

b_siyahjird.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, Kitab al-Masalik, p. 278, and Ibn Hawqal, p. 326, as Siyahjird/Siyahgird, irrigated by the Dahas/Balkhab river on the Balkh–Tirmidh road). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_siyahjird.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Siyāh-gird ('Black Town/Enclosure', Arabicized as Siyāhjird), a settlement in the Balkh oasis attested from the 10th century CE.

b_khulm.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, as Ho-lin / Khulm, a state 800 li in circuit with ten Buddhist monasteries); also recorded in early 8th-century CE Arab conquest narratives (al-Tabari).
b_khulm.etymology_analysis: Ancient Bactrian toponym Khulm (transcribed Ho-lin by Xuanzang c. 630 CE); later known as Tashqurghan in the 19th century CE before reverting to Khulm.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Khulm (ancient Bactrian city on the Silk Road) (in-game: Chulm)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from Valvalij.

b_andarab.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, as An-to-la-po / Andarab, one of the twelve constituent states of Tokharistan); later Abbasid mint from 871–872 CE.
b_andarab.etymology_analysis: Persian hydronymic compound andar-āb ('between the rivers/waters'), referring to the Andarab river and valley in Tokharistan.

b_baghlan.first_mention_attestation: c. 156 CE Kushan Bactrian inscription SK4 at Surkh Kotal (as bagolango, 'image-temple/sanctuary'); later attested by Xuanzang (c. 630 CE, as Fo-kia-lang).
b_baghlan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Bactrian bagolango ('image-temple / sanctuary', from Old Iranian *baga-dānaka-), attested at the Kushan dynastic sanctuary of Surkh Kotal and passing to the surrounding district.

b_valvalij.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, as Huo/Hwo, the Hephthalite/Western Turk capital of Tokharistan) and early 8th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (al-Tabari, as Warwaliz/Walwalij).

morphemes.translation: Warn / Aornos (ancient name of the city)

b_valvalij.etymology_analysis: Compound of the ancient Bactrian city name Warn (Greek Aornos) and Bactrian lizo ('fortress'), yielding Warwaliz / Walwalij (modern Kunduz, from Persian kuhandiz 'old fortress').

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Tokharestan capital Valvalij.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek accounts of Alexander the Great's 329 BCE Bactrian campaign (Arrian, Strabo).
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greco-Bactrian names for the site of Warwaliz/Kunduz prior to the compound Warwaliz.

b_talekan.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, as Ta-la-kien / Talikan) and early 8th-century CE Arab campaigns in Tokharistan (al-Tabari, c. 705–710 CE).
b_talekan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Iranian toponym Ṭāyaqān / Ṭālaqān (modern Taloqan), attested from the 7th century CE in Tokharistan.

b_mila.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, Kitab al-Masalik, p. 279, and Ibn Hawqal, p. 326, as Rubat Milan, a fortified guard-house at the Oxus bend near Khulm on the road from Balkh to Khuttal). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_mila.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Rubāt Mīlān, a fortified Oxus crossing guard-post three marches from Balkh attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies.

b_samanjan.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, as Sih-min-kien / Simingan) and 4th–8th-century CE Bactrian documents (as Simingan/Samingan); earlier Greco-Bactrian Eukratidia.
b_samanjan.etymology_analysis: Bactrian/Middle Iranian toponym Simingān / Samangān (modern Aybak/Samangan), attested in Xuanzang (c. 630 CE) and early Islamic sources.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Greco-Bactrian foundation attributed to King Eucratides I (r. c. 171–145 BCE), cited by Strabo and Ptolemy.
older_name_by_867.notes: Hellenistic name of the city prior to Samangan/Aybak.

b_saan.first_mention_attestation: c. 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, p. 322) and 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam, §23.62, as San, a town in Guzganan). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_saan.etymology_analysis: Toponym Sān (paired with Chāryak as Sān wa Chāryak, modern Sangcharak), first attested in late 10th-century CE geographical works.

b_ruy.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (Xuanzang, as Hi-lu-si-min-kien = Ruy-Simingan) and early 8th-century CE Arab campaigns in Tokharistan (al-Tabari, ii, 1219, as Ru'b).
b_ruy.etymology_analysis: Ancient Tokharistan town Rūy / Ru'b (modern Ru'i in Samangan), attested alongside Simingan in Xuanzang (c. 630 CE) and al-Tabari (early 8th century CE).

b_azadawan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Azadawan in Ghur/Darmashan.
b_azadawan.etymology_analysis: Persian-formed toponym (cf. āzād 'free/noble'), unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources for Ghur.

b_darmashan.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam, §23.48 and §24.12, as Darmashan/Varmashan, a mountainous region of Ghur ruled by the Darmashi-shah); later Juzjani (13th century CE). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_darmashan.etymology_analysis: Medieval regional name in Ghur (Darmashān / Dar-i Mašān / Varmashān), first attested in the 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Changazstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Changaz
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_zirjan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Zirjan in Ghur/Darmashan.

morphemes.translation: toponym (distinct from Zirjan villages in Nishapur/Gonabad)

b_zirjan.etymology_analysis: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources for Ghur or Darmashan.

b_firuzkuh.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1146 CE by Qutb al-Din Muhammad of the Ghurid dynasty as the Ghurid summer capital (recorded in Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri). No pre-1146 CE attestation.
b_firuzkuh.etymology_analysis: Persian oronym Fīrūzkūh ('Turquoise Mountain'), given to the Ghurid capital founded in 1146 CE.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_khasht.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, p. 267, 285; Ibn Hawqal, p. 318, 334; al-Muqaddasi, p. 298, 307, as Khasht, a town on the upper Hari Rud counted in Ghur). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_khasht.etymology_analysis: Town on the upper Hari Rud route into Ghur, first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works.

b_ahanjaran.first_mention_attestation: 1011 CE (campaigns of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni in Ghur, recorded by al-Utbi and Juzjani's Tabaqat-i Nasiri, as Ahangaran, the fortified capital of eastern Ghur). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ahanjaran.etymology_analysis: Persian Āhangarān ('[place of] the blacksmiths/ironworkers', Arabicized as Āhanjarān), reflecting Ghur's medieval ironworking and arms industry.

b_ghur.first_mention_attestation: 725 CE Umayyad campaign of Asad ibn Abdallah al-Qasri into Ghur (recorded in al-Tabari, Ta'rikh), following earlier Arab raids under Caliph Uthman (r. 644–656 CE).

morphemes.language: Eastern Iranian (cognate with Avestan gairi-, Sogdian gor-)

b_ghur.etymology_analysis: Derived from an Eastern Iranian root *gar- / *gōr- meaning 'mountain' (cognate with Avestan gairi- and Sogdian gor-), referring to the mountainous heartland of central Afghanistan.

b_dih-e-khalaf.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Dih-e-Khalaf in Upper Ghur.
b_dih-e-khalaf.etymology_analysis: Persian-Arabic compound meaning 'Village of Khalaf', unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources.

b_ribat-e-karyan.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam, §23.63, as Ribat-i Karvan/Kirvan, a frontier borough of Guzganan toward Ghur with gold mines in its mountains). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ribat-e-karyan.etymology_analysis: Persian-Arabic compound Ribāṭ-i Karvān ('Caravan Ribat'), first attested in the 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam on the Ghur–Guzgan frontier.

b_till.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam, §24.12, as Til, one of the two frontier fortresses of Zamin-Davar facing Ghur). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_till.etymology_analysis: Frontier fortress in Zamin-Davar on the southern border of Ghur, first attested in the 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam.

b_kusuy.first_mention_attestation: 891 CE (al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan, p. 278) and early 10th-century CE geographers (Ibn Rustah, p. 171; al-Istakhri, p. 267; Ibn Hawqal, p. 319, as Kusuy/Kusuyah near the Hari Rud). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kusuy.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan town Kūsūy / Kūsūyah near the Hari Rud, first attested in late 9th-century CE Arabic geographical literature.

b_bamain.first_mention_attestation: c. 1219–1224 CE (Yaqut al-Hamawi, Mu'jam al-Buldan, i, p. 481, 487, as Bamiyin/Bamanj, a town in Badghis near Babnah/Bavan). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bamain.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement in Badghis (distinct from Bamiyan), recorded by Yaqut al-Hamawi in the early 13th century CE.

b_jabal-al-fidda.first_mention_attestation: 764 CE (147 AH) and 772 CE (155 AH) Abbasid copper fals coins minted at Jabal al-Fidda ('Silver Mountain') in Badghis during and after the revolt of Ustad Sis; also 10th-century CE geographers (al-Istakhri, al-Muqaddasi, Hudud al-'Alam as Kuh-i Sim).
b_jabal-al-fidda.etymology_analysis: Arabic oronym Jabal al-Fiḍḍa ('Silver Mountain', rendered in Persian as Kūh-i Sīm in Hudud al-'Alam), referring to the silver-mining mountain and Abbasid mint in Badghis.

b_buzjan.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi, and 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam §23.19, as Buzjan/Buzhagan, chief town of the Zam/Jam district); also birthplace of Abu'l-Wafa al-Buzjani (b. 940 CE). No documented written attestation of Buzjan <= 867 CE (though the Zam district was conquered in 651–652 CE).
b_buzjan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan city Būzjān / Būzhagān (modern Buzhgan in Torbat-e Jam County), seat of the Zam (Jam) district in the 10th century CE.

b_pushang.first_mention_attestation: 588 CE Synod of Ishoyahb I (mentioning a Nestorian bishopric at Pushang/Bushang); later conquered by Arab forces in 652–653 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 405, 409; al-Tabari, ii, p. 79).
b_pushang.eponym_details: Medieval Iranian tradition attributed its foundation to the mythical hero Pashang (folk etymology) or to Sasanian king Shapur I (r. 240–270 CE).
b_pushang.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Pūšang (Arabicized as Būšanj / Fūšanj, modern Ghurian/Zinda Jan), an ancient Sasanian-era city west of Herat.

b_tayabad.first_mention_attestation: Late 14th century CE (associated with mystic Shaykh Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Taybadi, d. 1389 CE, and Timurid-era shrine built 1444 CE). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_tayabad.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym ending in -ābād ('settlement/cultivated place'), first prominent in late medieval and Timurid Khorasan sources.

b_khawaf.first_mention_attestation: 891 CE (al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan, p. 278) and early 10th-century CE geographers (Ibn Rustah, p. 171; al-Istakhri; Ibn Hawqal; al-Muqaddasi, as Khwaf/Khwab). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: district and town name in Kuhistan

b_khawaf.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym Khwāf (earlier Khwāb, modern Khaf), first attested in late 9th-century CE Arabic geographical works.

b_zurabad.first_mention_attestation: 1528 CE (site of the Safavid–Uzbek Battle of Jam at Zurabad in Khorasan). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_zurabad.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym ending in -ābād ('settlement/cultivated place') in the Jam/Bakharz region of Khorasan, unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_herat.first_mention_attestation: Achaemenid Old Persian royal inscriptions of Darius I (Behistun Inscription, c. 520 BCE) as Haraiva, and Greek historical accounts of Alexander the Great's campaign (330 BCE) as Aria and Artacoana.

morphemes.translation: well-watered land / Aria (region of the Hari River)

b_herat.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Haraiva (Avestan Harōiuua, Greek Aria), passing through Middle Persian Harēv/Harīy into New Persian Herāt. The name is cognate with the Hari Rud ('Hari River') and denotes a well-watered region.

b_karukh.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies, first in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.34), describing Karukh as a prosperous mountain borough northeast of Herat.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Herat highlands

b_karukh.etymology_analysis: Local Persian toponym (Karūkh/Karokh) for a mountain town 50 km northeast of Herat, attested by 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri and Hudud al-'Alam) as a prosperous district famous for raisins.

b_malin.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, pp. 256, 266) and Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE, p. 433), who explicitly distinguish Malin of Herat from Malin of Bakharz.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Herat oasis

b_malin.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym (Mālīn/Mālan) for a medieval town in the Herat oasis (near modern Malan south of Herat), explicitly distinguished by 10th-century CE geographers al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal from Malin in Bakharz.

b_asfuzar.first_mention_attestation: Late 8th-century CE Islamic historical accounts of Kharijite rebellions (al-Hudayn at the end of the 2nd/8th century and Hamza b. Adharak in the early 9th century CE, cited in Encyclopaedia Iranica) attesting the district and town of Asfezar (Asfuzar).

morphemes.translation: district and town name south of Herat

b_asfuzar.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym Asfezār (or Asfōzar/Asfusār), designating a fertile district (kūra) and chief town south of Herat on the Harut/Adraskand River; later renamed Sabzavār-i Herāt ('Green Place') and in modern times Shīndand (Pashto translation of Sabzavār).

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_adraskan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 267) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, p. 298) as Adraskar, Ibn Hawqal (pp. 439-40), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 29) as Araskan.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Asfezar district

b_adraskan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian toponym (attested as Adraskar in al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Muqaddasi, and Araskan in Hudud al-'Alam) for one of the four towns of the Asfezar district, situated on the Harut (Adraskand) River.

b_khin.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; appears only in modern/local toponymy as a constituent holding of Asfuzar.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name (unattested in early sources)

b_khin.etymology_analysis: Unattested in early Islamic or pre-Islamic geographical sources; used in the repository as a constituent holding of Asfuzar (Sabzevar of Herat).

b_abiz.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern town of Abiz-e Jadid in Zirkuh County, South Khorasan, Iran.
b_abiz.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym (Ābīz, glossed in Dehkhoda's dictionary as 'spark/ember of fire', locally associated with a former fire temple) in the Zirkuh district of Quhistan (South Khorasan, Iran), lacking any documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_shahrakht.first_mention_attestation: Post-867 CE; the surrounding Zirkuh/Petergan district of Quhistan is mentioned in 14th–15th century CE Ilkhanid and Timurid geographies (Hamdallah Mustawfi, c. 1340 CE; Hafiz-i Abru), with Shahrakht itself attested in later local records.
b_shahrakht.etymology_analysis: Persian compound toponym (Shāh-rakht) in the Petergan/Zirkuh district of South Khorasan, Iran; the surrounding region appears in Ilkhanid and Timurid geographies (14th–15th centuries CE), with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_amol-e-shatt.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (670 CE / 50 AH, al-Tabari), recording expeditions sent by the governor of Khorasan Rabi'a b. Ziyad al-Harithi to Amul and Zamm to secure the Oxus crossings.
b_amol-e-shatt.etymology_analysis: Early medieval designation Āmol-e Šaṭṭ ('Āmol on the river bank', also called Āmol-e Jayḥūn or Āmūya), distinguishing the Oxus crossing city (modern Türkmenabat) from Āmol in Mazandaran; attested in Arab conquest accounts from 670 CE.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Amûl-am-Oxus).

b_shagal.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; local settlement name in the Amul (Türkmenabat) oasis.
b_shagal.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Amul (Türkmenabat) oasis along the Amu Darya, lacking any documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sayat.first_mention_attestation: No documented pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern town of Saýat in Lebap Region, Turkmenistan, named after a Turkmen tribe.
b_sayat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sayat (Saýat) Turkmen tribe, ultimately derived from Arabic ṣayyād ('hunter'). Located 35 km southeast of Türkmenabat (Amul), with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_yahudan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 270), al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, p. 298), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.53), attesting Jahudhan / al-Yahudiyya (modern Maymana) as the capital of Guzgan.
b_yahudan.etymology_analysis: Persian Jahūdhān (Arabicized as al-Yahūdīya), meaning 'place of the Jews', attested by 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri, al-Muqaddasi, Hudud al-'Alam) as the capital of Guzgan (modern Maymana). No pre-867 CE written attestation of this toponym is documented.

b_andkhud.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE historical account in al-Tabari (II, p. 1566) for events of 116 AH / 734 CE (revolt of al-Harith ibn Surayj) as al-Nokhdh, and 10th-century CE geographies as Ankhudh (al-Istakhri) and Antkhodh (Hudud al-'Alam).
b_andkhud.etymology_analysis: Early medieval town in Guzgan (modern Andkhoy, Afghanistan), attested in al-Tabari (II, p. 1566) for events of 734 CE as al-Nokhdh and later by 10th-century geographers as Ankhudh (al-Istakhri), Antkhodh (Hudud al-'Alam), and Andakhudh (al-Muqaddasi).

b_faryab.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (652–653 CE / 32 AH, al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, pp. 406–407, and al-Tabari) recording the conquest of Faryab by Abdallah ibn Amir, and 665–666 CE governorship under Qays b. Haytham.
b_faryab.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym Fāryāb (also Pāryāb, Bāryāb), meaning 'land irrigated by diversion of river water'. Attested in Arab conquest accounts of 652–653 CE (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari) and later attributed by Gardizi to the Sasanian king Peroz I.

b_taleqan.first_mention_attestation: 7th- and 8th-century CE historical accounts in al-Tabari (45 AH / 665–666 CE governorship of Qays b. Haytham over Marv-al-Rud, Talaqan, and Faryab; and 90–91 AH / 709–710 CE, Tabari II, p. 1218, mentioning Sohrak, king of Talaqan).
b_taleqan.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the western threshold of Guzgan (distinct from Talaqan in Tokharistan), attested in al-Tabari for 665–666 CE and 709–710 CE during the Arab campaigns in Guzgan and Tokharistan.

b_gurzivan.first_mention_attestation: Late 9th-century CE geography of al-Ya'qubi (Kitab al-Buldan, 891 CE, p. 287) as Qorzoman, and 10th-century CE geographies (Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi, Hudud al-'Alam 982 CE) as Gorzevan / Jorzovan.
b_gurzivan.etymology_analysis: Town in the mountainous headwaters of Guzgan (summer capital of the Farighunid princes), first attested as Qorzomān by al-Ya'qubi (891 CE) and later as Gorzevān/Jorzovān in 10th-century CE geographies (Ibn Hawqal, Hudud al-'Alam); postdates the 867 CE baseline.

b_anbar-guzgani.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE historical account in al-Tabari (II, p. 1773) and Yaqut (I, p. 259), recording that the Alid pretender Yahya ibn Zayd was killed at Anbar in Guzgan in 125 AH / 743 CE.
b_anbar-guzgani.etymology_analysis: From Middle/New Persian anbār ('storehouse, granary'), qualified as Anbār of Guzgan (probably modern Sar-e Pol, Afghanistan). Attested in al-Tabari (II, p. 1773) for 743 CE as the site where Yahya ibn Zayd was killed, and later served as the winter capital of the Farighunids.

b_marv-ar-rud.first_mention_attestation: 6th-century CE Syriac ecclesiastical records attesting a Nestorian Christian bishopric at Marw-Rud in 553 CE, followed by 652 CE Arab conquest accounts (al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri) recording the submission of its marzban Badham.
b_marv-ar-rud.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Marwirōd (Arabicized Marw al-Rūdh), meaning 'Merv on the river' (the Murghab), distinguishing it from Great Merv (Marw al-Shāhijān). Attested as a Nestorian bishopric in 553 CE and in 652 CE Arab conquest accounts.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Merwe-ar-Rût).

b_qarinayn.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th-century CE administrative geography of Qudama ibn Ja'far (Kitab al-Kharaj, p. 209) mentioning the Zoroastrians (majus) in Qarinayn, followed by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE).

morphemes.translation: the two joined/paired ones (dual of qarīn)

b_qarinayn.etymology_analysis: Arabic dual form Qarīnayn ('the two joined/paired ones'), applied to the town on the Murghab River between Merv and Marv-ar-Rud because it was reckoned sometimes to Merv and sometimes to Marv-ar-Rud. Attested in 10th-century CE sources (Qudama ibn Ja'far, al-Istakhri).

b_barkdiz.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Persian geography Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.40, as *Barakdiz) and 12th-century CE biographical dictionary of al-Sam'ani, describing it as a fortified settlement on the Murghab River.
b_barkdiz.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym ending in -diz ('fortress'), attested in Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE) as a fortified settlement on the Murghab River inhabited by Bihafaridhi Zoroastrians, and noted by al-Sam'ani (12th century CE) as the earlier local name of Qarinayn.

b_panjdih.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE geographical dictionary of Yaqut al-Hamawi (Mu'jam al-Buldan, c. 1225 CE) attesting Panjdih (Arabicized Fanjdih / Khams Qura) on the Murghab River.
b_panjdih.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Panj-dih ('Five Villages', Arabicized as Fanjdih or translated as Khams Qurā), referring to an oasis settlement on the Murghab River (modern Tagtabazar, Turkmenistan). Attested in post-867 medieval geographies (Yaqut al-Hamawi, 13th century CE).

b_baghshur.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 269), al-Muqaddasi, and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.33), describing Baghshur on the steppe between Herat and Marv-ar-Rud.
b_baghshur.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym Bāghshūr (also glossed as 'pool of salt water', referring to its brackish wells on the steppe between Herat and Merv), attested in 10th-century CE geographies (al-Istakhri, al-Muqaddasi, Hudud al-'Alam) and as the birthplace of scholar al-Baghawi (1042 CE).

b_merv.first_mention_attestation: Achaemenid Old Persian royal inscriptions of Darius I (Behistun Inscription, c. 515 BCE) as Margu, and the Avestan Vendidad as Mouru.
b_merv.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Margu (Avestan Mouru, Greek Margianē), becoming Middle Persian Marv (Arabic Marw al-Shāhijān). Attested in the Behistun Inscription of Darius I (c. 515 BCE) and refounded under the Seleucids as Alexandria / Antiochia Margiana.

b_sinj.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 263) as Sinj, al-Muqaddasi (p. 299), and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.43) as Shing-i 'Abbadi in the Merv oasis.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Merv oasis

b_sinj.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in the Merv oasis, first attested by 10th-century CE Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri as Sinj, Hudud al-'Alam as Shing-i 'Abbādī); postdates the 867 CE baseline.

b_jiranj.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 263) as Jiranj and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.41) as Girang in the Merv oasis.

morphemes.translation: small town in the Merv oasis

b_jiranj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form Jīranj (also Jīrjanj) of Persian Gīrang/Kīrang, a small town in the Merv oasis attested by 10th-century CE geographers (al-Istakhri, Hudud al-'Alam); postdates the 867 CE baseline.

b_kharad.first_mention_attestation: Late 10th-century CE Islamic geography of al-Muqaddasi (Ahsan al-Taqasim, c. 985 CE) listing Kharaq (variant Kharad) among the dependencies of Merv.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Merv oasis

b_kharad.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement in the Merv oasis (corresponding to Kharaq/Kharad in al-Muqaddasi's 10th-century CE list of Merv dependencies), with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_shawashkan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 263) as Sausaqan, Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.45) as Susanaqan, and Yaqut (III, p. 245) as Shavashkan.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Merv oasis

b_shawashkan.etymology_analysis: Medieval borough in the Merv oasis attested from the 10th century CE onward (as Sausaqān in al-Istakhri, Sūsanaqān in Hudud al-'Alam, and Shavashkān in Yaqut); postdates the 867 CE baseline.

b_kushmaihan.first_mention_attestation: Early Islamic historical narrative in al-Tabari (Tarikh, Vol. 5) attesting Kushmayhan as a village in the Merv oasis, and 10th-century CE geographies (al-Istakhri, p. 263; Hudud al-'Alam, sec. 23.45).
b_kushmaihan.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian compound toponym (Kūš-mayhan, 'pavilion/castle abode') for a major irrigated village in the Merv oasis, attested in al-Tabari's historical narrative (Sasanian/early Islamic Merv) and 10th-century CE geographers.

b_dizah.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 270) and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.37) as Diza, a borough on the upper Murghab River.
b_dizah.etymology_analysis: From Middle/New Persian diza ('fortress, walled settlement'), a borough on the upper Murghab River in the Marv-ar-Rud/Gharjistan borderlands, first attested in 10th-century CE geographies (al-Istakhri, Hudud al-'Alam).

b_bashin.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Armenian Geography (Ashkharhatsuyts) as Abzhin, and 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, p. 271; Hudud al-'Alam, sec. 23.36) as Abshin/Bashin, chief town of Gharjistan.

morphemes.language: Middle Iranian (via Armenian Abzhin / Arabic Bashīn)

b_bashin.etymology_analysis: One of the two chief towns of Gharjistan (Gharj al-Shar) on the upper Murghab River, attested as Abzhin in the 7th-century CE Armenian Geography (Ashkharhatsuyts) and later as Abshīn/Bashīn in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies.

b_shurmin.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographies: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 271), Ibn Hawqal, and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE, sec. 23.35) as Surmin/Shurmin in Gharjistan.
b_shurmin.etymology_analysis: One of the two chief towns of Gharjistan (Gharj al-Shar) alongside Bashin, first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, Hudud al-'Alam); postdates the 867 CE baseline.

b_sarakhs.first_mention_attestation: Late 6th- to 7th-century CE Sasanian administrative clay bullae (580–650 CE) excavated at Aq Tepe near Sarakhs, and 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (c. 652 CE, Ibn A'tham II, p. 104, naming Abraz as marzban of Sarakhs).

morphemes.translation: oasis city on the lower Hari Rud (Tedzhen)

b_sarakhs.etymology_analysis: Ancient oasis city on the lower Hari Rud (Tedzhen) along the Silk Road between Nishapur and Merv. Sasanian administrative bullae (580–650 CE) from Aq Tepe and early Islamic conquest accounts (652 CE) attest Sarakhs; Ferdowsi's Shahnameh gives a legendary eponymous foundation by Sarakhs son of Godarz.

b_dandanqan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dandānqān by Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, pp. 24, 202; first recension c. 846 CE) as a small fortified town in the Qara Qum desert between Merv and Sarakhs.
b_dandanqan.etymology_analysis: Persian/Iranian toponym (Dandānqān), formed with the toponymic suffix -qān/-gān; later famous as the site of the 1040 CE Battle of Dandanaqan between the Seljuks and Ghaznavids.

b_shiraz-sarakhsi.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_shiraz-sarakhsi.etymology_analysis: Compound of Shiraz and the nisba Sarakhsi ('of Sarakhs'); no documented historical settlement of this name is attested in the Sarakhs oasis by 867 CE.

b_zamm.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 673 CE (53 AH) when Arab forces under 'Abd Allah ibn Rabi' al-Harithi established tribute agreements with the fortified Oxus crossing town of Zamm (recorded in al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri).
b_zamm.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic and pre-Islamic Iranian toponym (Zamm, Arabicized from Sām/Zām), a major fortified crossing point on the western bank of the Oxus (Amu Darya), corresponding to modern Kerki in Turkmenistan.

b_niyaz.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_niyaz.etymology_analysis: Derived from Persian niyāz ('need, desire, supplication'); no documented historical settlement named Niyaz is attested in the Zamm/Oxus region by 867 CE.

b_abivard.first_mention_attestation: Identifiable with Parthian Apauarktikē mentioned by Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations, c. 1st century CE); later attested as a Sasanian Nestorian bishopric at the synod of 553 CE and conquered by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir in 651–652 CE.
b_abivard.eponym_details: Legendarily attributed by Yaqut al-Hamawi to Bāvard, son of Gūdarz (a mythical Iranian hero of the Shahnameh tradition, pre-867 CE).
b_abivard.etymology_analysis: From Parthian Apauarktikē (Middle Persian Abīvard / Bāvard), containing the Iranian element -vard ('enclosure, walled town'); a key frontier fortress town in northern Khorasan.

b_shahrastan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Shahrastāna in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE) among the towns of the district of Nasa in northern Khorasan, and later in Khwarazmian campaigns (1165 CE).
b_shahrastan.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian šahrestān ('provincial capital, walled city'); the specific settlement in the Nasa/Abivard district is first attested in 10th-century Islamic geography (c. 985 CE), post-867 CE.

b_nasa.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Parthian city of Nisa (Nisaia/Parthaunisa), founded c. 250–211 BCE and renamed Mithradātkert under Mithridates I (r. c. 171–138 BCE), attested in Parthian ostraca, Classical writers (Isidore of Charax, Strabo, Pliny), and early Islamic conquest accounts (650–651 CE).
b_nasa.etymology_analysis: From Old/Middle Iranian Nisā / Nisaia (Arabicized as Nasā), an ancient Parthian royal center in northern Khorasan (near modern Ashgabat, Turkmenistan).

b_khabushan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Khabūshān in 10th-century Islamic geographers (al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE; al-Hakim al-Nishaburi) as the chief town of the district of Ustuwa (modern Quchan).
b_khabushan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian toponym Khabūshān (later renamed Qūchān), serving as the Islamic-era urban center of the ancient Astauene/Ustuwa valley.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations (c. 1st century CE, recording Parthian royal city Asaak in Astauene/Ustuwa)
older_name_by_867.notes: Astauene (Arabic Ustuwa) and its Parthian capital Asaak lay in the immediate Quchan/Khabushan valley before Khabushan emerged as the medieval town name.

b_farava.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, p. 273), Ibn Hawqal (978 CE), Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE), though later tradition ascribed its ribat to governor 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir (828–845 CE).
b_farava.etymology_analysis: Frontier fortress (ribāt) of Farāva (Parau / Afrāva) on the northern Kopet-Dag edge facing the Karakum desert (modern Serdar/Kizyl-Arvat); earliest surviving written attestation is mid-10th century CE.

b_hesare-taq.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_hesare-taq.etymology_analysis: Persian descriptive compound Hesār-e Tāq ('Fortress/Enclosure of the Arch'); no documented written attestation exists by 867 CE.

b_keshmar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in connection with the famous Cypress of Kashmar felled in 861 CE (247 AH) by order of Abbasid Caliph al-Mutawakkil (recorded by Zakariya al-Qazwini and in Shahnameh tradition), and associated with the Sasanian/Parthian fire temple tradition.
b_keshmar.etymology_analysis: Historical Iranian town of Keshmar (modern Kashmar) in the Turshiz/Busht district of Khorasan; also known in medieval Islamic geography as Turshiz.

b_sabzavar.first_mention_attestation: The name Sabzavār (also Sūzavār) is first attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers (Hudud al-'Alam, 982 CE; al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE) as the chief town of the Bayhaq district.
b_sabzavar.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Sabzavār ('verdant/green place'); while the district and town of Bayhaq is attested from 650–651 CE, the specific name Sabzavar appears in 10th-century sources.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan / Ibn Funduq, Tarikh-i Bayhaq (30 AH / 650–651 CE surrender to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir)
older_name_by_867.notes: Bayhaq was the earlier name of the town and rural district before Sabzavar became the standard urban name.

b_mazinan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a station along the southern Great Khorasan Road between Qumis and Bayhaq/Sabzavar in medieval Islamic itineraries (al-Muqaddasi / al-Idrisi; 10th century CE onward).
b_mazinan.etymology_analysis: Iranian toponym Mazīnān (also historically associated with Bahmanabad on the Khorasan Road west of Sabzevar); no written attestation <= 867 CE verified.
