b_damghan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest references to the name Dāmghān date to the mid-9th century CE (Qudama ibn Ja'far, Kitab al-Kharaj; al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Ya'qubi) and the devastating 20 December 856 CE Damghan earthquake.
b_damghan.eponym_details: Legendarily ascribed by Persian historiographers to the mythical Pishdadian king Hushang (pre-867 CE).
b_damghan.etymology_analysis: Uncertain origin, traditionally explained as a contraction of Persian deh-e moghān ('village of the Magi'); capital of medieval Qumis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical historians of Alexander the Great (330 BCE) and Strabo / Pliny
older_name_by_867.notes: Shahr-e Qumis (ancient Hecatompylos), ~26–32 km southwest of Damghan, was the earlier capital of Qumis before Damghan replaced it.

b_biyar.first_mention_attestation: Earliest detailed attestation is by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE, Ahsan al-Taqasim, pp. 26, 356–357), whose maternal grandfather came from Biyar, alongside 10th-century Samanid coins.

morphemes.translation: Arabic plural of biʾr: well, spring

b_biyar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic biʾār ('wells, springs'), referring to its qanat-fed water supply on the northern fringe of the Dasht-e Kavir (modern Beyarjomand).

b_bistum.first_mention_attestation: Attested by the mid-9th century CE as Bastām/Bistām in Qumis: birthplace and home of Sufi mystic Bayazid Bastami (804–874 CE) and affected by the 856 CE Damghan/Qumis earthquake.
b_bistum.eponym_details: Traditionally attributed to Vistāhm (Bistām), uncle of Sasanian king Khosrau II (late 6th century CE, pre-867 CE).
b_bistum.etymology_analysis: Named after the late Sasanian prince Vistāhm (Bistām), who revolted against Khosrau II in the 590s CE; situated 6 km north of Shahrud in Qumis.

b_gerdkuh.first_mention_attestation: Earliest known reference dates to the early 10th century CE (c. 934 CE), when it served as the residence of Isma'ili da'i 'Abd al-Malik Kawkabi (successor to Abu Hatim Razi, d. 934 CE).
b_gerdkuh.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Gerdkūh ('Round Mountain'), named after the dome-shaped isolated rocky hill 18 km west of Damghan; later a major Nizari Isma'ili fortress.

b_nishapur.first_mention_attestation: Founded or rebuilt in the 3rd century CE (c. 250 CE) by Sasanian king Shapur I as Nēw-Šāhpūr, administrative capital of Abarshahr; conquered by Arabs in 651–652 CE and made Tahirid capital in 830 CE.
b_nishapur.eponym_details: Named after Sasanian king Shapur I (r. 240–270 CE), from Middle Persian Nēw-Šāhpūr ('Fair/Good City of Shapur').
b_nishapur.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Nēw-Šāhpūr ('Good City of Shapur'), Arabicized as Naysābūr and New Persian Nīshāpūr; also known in Sasanian times by the provincial name Abarshahr.

b_zawa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zāwa (Zaveh) in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (d. 892 CE) among the districts of Nishapur conquered by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir in 30–31 AH (651–652 CE).
b_zawa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan district and town of Zāwa (Zaveh), later renamed Torbat-e Heydarieh after the 13th-century Sufi Qutb al-Din Haydar (d. c. 1230 CE).

b_shamat.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Shāmāt, one of the four rural quarters (rub') of the Nishapur district, in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE) and al-Hakim al-Nishaburi's Tarikh-i Nishabur (d. 1014 CE).
b_shamat.etymology_analysis: Historical quarter (rub') of Nishapur (surviving in modern Rob-e Shamat Rural District); earliest surviving written attestation is late 10th century CE.

b_farhajird.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Farjird/Fargard on Ibn Hawqal's map (Surat al-Ard, c. 978 CE) and in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as the chief town of the Asfand district of Nishapur.
b_farhajird.eponym_details: Traditionally attributed to Farhād (Farhād-gerd, 'built/made by Farhad', a pre-867 Iranian name).
b_farhajird.etymology_analysis: From Middle/New Persian Farhād-gerd (Arabicized as Farhādjird / Farhajird), containing the Iranian suffix -gerd ('built by / town of'); earliest written attestation is 10th century CE.

b_rivand.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Avesta as Mount Raēvant (site of the sacred fire Adur Burzen-Mihr in Parthian/Sasanian Bundahishn tradition), and later as one of the four quarters (rub') of Nishapur.
b_rivand.etymology_analysis: From Avestan Raēvant ('splendid, rich'), originally the name of Mount Rivand (Kūh-e Rīvand) near Nishapur, which gave its name to the surrounding quarter and town.

b_samaiqan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th–11th century sources as Samanqān / Samalqān (al-Muqaddasi c. 985 CE as Sefinqān under Nasa; Ibn Sina's 1012 CE journey through Samangan/Samanqan to Gorgan).
b_samaiqan.etymology_analysis: Samaiqan is a scribal/OCR variant of Samalqān (medieval Samanqān), a district and town in North Khorasan; earliest surviving written attestation is late 10th century CE.

b_jarmaqan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jarmaqān in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE) among the towns of the Nasa district in northern Khorasan (corresponding to modern Garmeh).
b_jarmaqan.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Jarmaqān) of Iranian Garmagān / Garmeh ('warm place'); earliest written attestation is al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).

b_dawin.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_dawin.etymology_analysis: No documented historical settlement named Dawin is attested in the Samalqan/North Khorasan region by 867 CE.

b_tus.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tūs in Sasanian and 5th-century Syriac Christian records (and earlier as Greek Susia in 330 BCE); conquered by Umayyads in the 7th century and site of Caliph Harun al-Rashid's death in 809 CE.
b_tus.eponym_details: Legendarily attributed in the Shahnameh tradition to Tūs, son of Nowzar (mythical Iranian hero, pre-867 CE).
b_tus.etymology_analysis: Ancient Khorasan city of Tūs, succeeding or identified with Classical Susia; famous in the Islamic era as the birthplace of Ferdowsi and al-Ghazali.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Diodorus Siculus, and Curtius (330 BCE Alexander campaigns in Aria/Parthia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Known to the ancient Greeks as Susia (Σούσια) when Alexander the Great passed through in 330 BCE.

b_mazduran.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Islamic road itineraries along the northeastern Great Khorasan Road between Tus/Mashhad and Sarakhs (e.g., Mazdūrān / Mozdūrān pass and station, 10th century CE onward).
b_mazduran.etymology_analysis: Persian Mazdūrān / Mozdūrān, a mountain pass and caravan station between Tus and Sarakhs; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE verified.

b_maihana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mayhana (Mahana/Mihana), chef-lieu of Khawaran in northern Khorasan, in al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) and as the birthplace of Sufi master Abu Sa'id ibn Abi'l-Khayr in 967 CE.
b_maihana.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan town of Mayhana (modern Meana in Turkmenistan) in the Khawaran district near Abivard and Sarakhs; earliest written attestation is late 10th century CE.

b_nuqaq.first_mention_attestation: Variant/corrupt form of Nūqān, one of the twin towns of Tus (alongside Tabaran), explicitly attested by al-Ya'qubi (Kitab al-Buldan, c. 891 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).
b_nuqaq.etymology_analysis: Nuqaq is a scribal/game-map corruption of Nūqān, the medieval city of Tus near Sanabad (modern Mashhad); earliest surviving written attestation of the name Nūqān is al-Ya'qubi (c. 891 CE).

b_jajarm.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written attestation is in al-Muqaddasi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (c. 985 CE, p. 300) as a small, prosperous district and town of Nishapur between Juwain and Gorgan (absent from al-Istakhri).
b_jajarm.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan town of Jājarm on the northern branch of the Great Khorasan Road; although prehistoric Tepe Pahlavan lies nearby, written attestation begins in the late 10th century CE.

b_isfarain.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Asbarā'īn (Esfarāyen) in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (d. 892 CE) among the districts of Nishapur conquered by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir in 30–31 AH (651–652 CE).
b_isfarain.eponym_details: Legendarily attributed to the Iranian epic hero Esfandiyār (pre-867 CE), with a folk etymology 'shield bearers' (Siparāyin) noted by Yaqut.
b_isfarain.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khorasan district and town of Esfarāyen (Isfarā'īn); Yaqut notes a folk etymology 'shield bearers' and an alleged earlier name Mehrjān (unattested pre-867 CE).

b_bint.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Bent (Bint) appears in 19th-20th century CE gazetteers and modern Iranian administrative records as a regional center in Makran.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name (uncertain etymology; possibly related to Balochi/Persian band 'embankment, dam')

b_bint.etymology_analysis: Modern Balochi and Persian toponym Bent (romanized as Bint) in Nik Shahr County, Sistan and Baluchestan. Its etymology is uncertain, possibly connected to Iranian band ('embankment, dam') or a local Balochi topographic term.

b_ruhna.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found in classical or Islamic geographical sources.
b_ruhna.etymology_analysis: Unattested in classical and early Islamic geographical literature for Makran and Kirman; etymology cannot be established from documented historical sources.

b_tiz.first_mention_attestation: Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) attests the port as Tēsa in the bay of Chabahar; later Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi, and Hudud al-Alam, 10th century CE) record it as Tīz, the chief maritime port of Makran.

morphemes.translation: coastal port name (Greek Tēsa; possibly related to Iranian *tēz 'sharp, promontory' or pre-Iranian substrate)

b_tiz.etymology_analysis: Ancient coastal emporium (modern Tis, near Chabahar) attested as Tēsa in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and as Tīz in medieval Islamic geographies, possibly reflecting an Iranian root *tēz ('sharp, point/promontory') or an older coastal substrate name.

b_bih.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), who mention Bih (Beh) as a district and town in Makran.
b_bih.etymology_analysis: Recorded in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works as Bih (Beh), a territory and town in Makran; the name corresponds to Persian bih/beh ('good, fertile').

b_bampur.first_mention_attestation: The medieval name Bampūr (Banbūr/Barbūr) is first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE; the earlier classical site Pura is attested in Arrian's Anabasis Alexandri (c. 140 CE).
b_bampur.etymology_analysis: Modern Bampur (Balochi Bunpūr) sits near a 3rd-millennium BCE archaeological mound and is widely identified with Pura, the Achaemenid/Gedrosian capital visited by Alexander the Great in 325 BCE (recorded by Arrian, c. 140 CE). The later name Bampūr appears in 10th-century CE Islamic geography.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Cothildasburch — Disambiguated capital foundation: Feudal fortress seat established by Cothilda
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Anabasis Alexandri VI.24 (c. 140 CE, describing events of 325 BCE), naming Pura as the capital of Gedrosia.
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greek name for the capital of Gedrosia, generally identified with Bampur (40 km west of Iranshahr).

b_fahraj.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attests Fahraj of Bampur (modern Iranshahr, locally Pahrah) under the form Fahl Fahrah, distinct from Fahraj of Narmasir in Kirman.
b_fahraj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Fahraj / Fahl Fahrah) of Middle Persian Pahra (Balochi Pahrah, 'guardpost, watchtower'), located 15 miles east of Bampur in Makran and renamed Iranshahr in the 20th century CE.

b_jask.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Jask first appears in medieval Arabic and Persian sources from the late 11th-12th century CE (such as al-'Awtabi's Kitab Ansab al-'Arab) and later Hormuz chronicles.

morphemes.translation: coastal settlement name of uncertain origin

b_jask.etymology_analysis: Port town on the Gulf of Oman in Hormozgan (Persian Jāsk, Balochi Jāšk). The name's origin is uncertain and lacks documented written attestation before 867 CE.

b_manujan.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) describes Manukan (modern Manujan) in southern Kirman as 'the Basrah of Kirman' for its commercial importance.
b_manujan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian Manūkān/Manūqān (modern Manujan) in southern Kerman Province, attested in late 10th-century CE Islamic geography; the root is uncertain, with the Iranian locative suffix -ān.

b_darhafan.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attests Darhfan / Darahkan as a town in the Jiroft district (khūrah) of Kirman, one march from Manujan toward the coast.
b_darhafan.etymology_analysis: Unidentified medieval town in southern Kirman (recorded by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE as Darahkan/Darhfan), known for indigo cultivation; likely contains Persian dar ('gate, valley') with an obscure second element.

b_houn.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found in classical or Islamic geographical sources for Kirman or Makran.
b_houn.etymology_analysis: Unattested in classical and medieval Islamic geographical sources for Kirman and Makran; etymology is unknown.

b_south_jaz_murian.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation for the name 'Jaz Murian' (the modern English directional label 'South Jaz Murian' is contemporary); Zoroastrian Middle Persian scriptures (Bundahishn, c. 9th century CE) refer to the basin as Chitro Mêyân.

morphemes.translation: endorheic basin and seasonal lake name

b_south_jaz_murian.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional designation for the southern part of the Hamun-e Jaz Murian endorheic depression straddling Kerman and Sistan-Baluchestan. In Zoroastrian Middle Persian texts (Bundahishn), the basin was known as Chitro Mêyân.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Zoroastrian Middle Persian scriptures (Bundahishn, c. 9th century CE), calling the basin Chitro Mêyân.
older_name_by_867.notes: Middle Persian Zoroastrian name for the Jaz Murian basin; the modern directional label 'South Jaz Murian' is post-medieval.

b_riqan.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) describes the fortifications and Great Mosque of Rikan (Righan/Riqan), twenty miles south of Fahraj in Kirman.
b_riqan.etymology_analysis: Persian Rīgān (Arabicized Rīqān/Rīkān), derived from rīg ('sand') + -ān, referring to the sandy desert margin southeast of Bam in Kerman Province.

b_north_jaz_murian.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation for the name 'Jaz Murian' (the modern English directional label 'North Jaz Murian' is contemporary); Zoroastrian Middle Persian scriptures (Bundahishn, c. 9th century CE) refer to the basin as Chitro Mêyân.

morphemes.translation: endorheic basin and seasonal lake name

b_north_jaz_murian.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional designation for the northern part of the Hamun-e Jaz Murian endorheic depression in southeastern Iran. In Zoroastrian Middle Persian texts (Bundahishn), the basin was known as Chitro Mêyân.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Northern endorheic depression of the pre-867 Jaz Murian basin in Kirman (in-game: North Jaz Murian)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor North Jaz Murian fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Nord-Jaz-Murjân.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Zoroastrian Middle Persian scriptures (Bundahishn, c. 9th century CE), calling the basin Chitro Mêyân.
older_name_by_867.notes: Middle Persian Zoroastrian name for the Jaz Murian basin; the modern directional label 'North Jaz Murian' is post-medieval.

b_kurk.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attests Kurk (coupled with Bahar) between Righan and Bam in Kirman as a populous town surrounded by palm-groves.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (homonymous with Persian kurk 'fine underwool/down')

b_kurk.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement between Bam and Rigan in Kerman Province, first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_khawr.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for a specific settlement named Khawr in eastern Makran.
b_khawr.etymology_analysis: Arabic and Persian geographical term khawr ('tidal creek, inlet, lagoon'), used as a coastal toponym along the Makran and Persian Gulf littoral.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_rodkhan.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attests Rudhkan as a populous town in Kirman surrounded by date palms and orange-trees, likely on the Rudkhanah-i-Duzdi.
b_rodkhan.etymology_analysis: Persian Rūdkān/Rūdhkān ('river channel/bed'), attested by al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) for a town along a river course in southern Kirman.

b_kokahdan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found in classical or Islamic geographical sources.
b_kokahdan.etymology_analysis: Unattested in classical and early Islamic geographical sources for Makran; appears to contain an Iranian -dān locative suffix with an obscure first element.

b_qanbali.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) describe Qanbali (Kanbali) as a prosperous trading city two days' march from Armabil in eastern Makran.

morphemes.translation: coastal trading town name (identified with Khayrokot in Las Bela)

b_qanbali.etymology_analysis: Medieval port and commercial town in eastern Makran (Las Bela region, identified by Holdich with Khayrokot), first attested by 10th-century CE Arabic geographers.

b_armabil.first_mention_attestation: al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (d. 892 CE) and the Chachnama record that Muhammad ibn al-Qasim subdued Armabil by treaty (sulh) in 711 CE during his conquest of Makran and Sindh.

morphemes.translation: town name in eastern Makran (identified with Las Bela)

b_armabil.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic rendering of a pre-Islamic town in eastern Makran (identified with Las Bela in Pakistani Balochistan), conquered by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim in 711 CE and later described by al-Istakhri and al-Muqaddasi.

b_kiz.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE, cited by Yaqut for the Ma'danid ruler 'Isa ibn Ma'dan), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), Hudud al-Alam (982 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attest Kij/Kiz (modern Kech/Turbat) as a principal city of Makran.

morphemes.translation: regional and urban center of the Kech valley

b_kiz.etymology_analysis: Arabicized Kīz/Kīj of Balochi Kēč (modern Kech/Turbat), the main urban center of central Makran and seat of the Ma'danid dynasty in the 10th century CE.

b_rasak.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attest Rask as a notable town in Makran within the fertile district of al-Kharuj.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Sarbaz valley

b_rasak.etymology_analysis: Medieval Makrani town (modern Rask in Sistan and Baluchestan, Iran), first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works as Rāsk.

b_jiwani.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Jiwani is a modern fishing and commercial port in Gwadar District, Balochistan, Pakistan.
b_jiwani.etymology_analysis: Balochi coastal town and port at the eastern end of Gwatar Bay in Gwadar District, Pakistan, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_dizak_makrani.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) list Dazak (Dizak) among the towns of Makran.
b_dizak_makrani.etymology_analysis: From Persian/Balochi dizak ('little fortress'), historically applied to the Saravan valley in Persian Makran; attested as Dazak in 10th-century CE Islamic geographies.

b_bannajbur.first_mention_attestation: al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (d. 892 CE) records that Muhammad ibn al-Qasim subdued Fannazbur (Bannajbur) in 711 CE, and Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) lists it as the capital of Makran fourteen stages east of Fahraj.
b_bannajbur.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic transliteration (Fannazbūr / Bannajbūr) of modern Panjgur in Balochistan, Pakistan, whose name is explained in Balochi either as panj + goran ('five highlands') or panj + goor ('five graves').

b_saindak.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Saindak is a modern mining settlement in Chagai District, Balochistan, developed after copper-gold deposits were discovered in the 1970s CE.
b_saindak.etymology_analysis: Modern village and copper-gold mining site in Chagai District, Balochistan, Pakistan, with no pre-modern written attestation.

b_chagai.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Chagai appears in modern Balochistan administrative and geographical records.
b_chagai.etymology_analysis: Town and district in northwestern Balochistan, Pakistan, adjacent to the Chagai Hills; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_jalk.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) attests Jalk (modern Jaleq) as a station on the northern Makran route between Qusdar and Juy-Sulayman.
b_jalk.etymology_analysis: Iran's easternmost town (modern Jaleq in Golshan County, Sistan and Baluchestan), attested in 985 CE by al-Muqaddasi as Jālk.

b_mashki.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Mashki (Mashkel/Mashkid); archaeological burials in the valley (Nikoderian/Mashkel tombs) date to c. 800 CE, while the name appears in modern geography.

morphemes.translation: river and valley name in Makran

b_mashki.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Mashkel (Mashkid) River, which drains eastern Makran into the Mashkel Hamun; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_sanij.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) records Sanij (Sanig, also called Isbidh/Ispi, modern Nasratabad) and gives the stages in leagues along the desert road from Narmasir via Fahraj to Sanij.
b_sanij.etymology_analysis: Medieval desert oasis between Kirman and Sistan (also known in Balochi as Ispi/Isbidh and in modern times as Nasratabad), attested in Ibn Khordadbeh's mid-9th-century CE itinerary.

b_qantarat_kirman.first_mention_attestation: al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) attests Qantarat Kirman ('the Bridge of Kirman') as a ribat (guard-house) built by the Saffarid amir 'Amr ibn al-Layth (r. 879-901 CE) between Gavnishak and Kundur, south of Zaranj.

morphemes.translation: bridge, arched causeway (used here for a desert ribat/guard-house)

b_qantarat_kirman.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qanṭarat Kirmān ('the Bridge of Kirman'), a post-867 CE desert guard-house (ribāṭ) built by 'Amr ibn al-Layth al-Saffar (r. 879-901 CE) on the route between Kirman and Zaranj.

b_ladhir.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found in classical or Islamic geographical sources.
b_ladhir.etymology_analysis: Unattested in classical and medieval Islamic geographical sources for Makran, Kirman, and Sistan; etymology is unknown.

b_khwash.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 978 CE; al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE), which record Khwash (or Khwas) as a town on the Kirman-Makran borderland famous for sugarcane and panidh sugar.

morphemes.translation: pleasant, good, or sweet (historical oasis town)

b_khwash.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian Khwash (modern Khash, also recorded as Khwas and Vasht/Washt), an oasis town in the Sarhad district on the Kirman-Makran frontier. While local traditions associate the area with Sasanian-era Washt, the earliest documented written attestations of the settlement appear in 10th-century CE Islamic geographers.

b_qusdar.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (al-Istakhri, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 978 CE; al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE) and Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE), which describe Qusdar/Qozdar as the chief town of Turan.
b_qusdar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Islamic toponym Quzdar/Qusdar (modern Khuzdar in Balochistan, Pakistan). Although the surrounding region of Turan appears in accounts of Ardashir I's Sasanian-era campaigns (recorded later by al-Tabari), the town of Qusdar itself is first attested in writing by 10th-century CE Arab geographers.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_wad.first_mention_attestation: Late 15th-century CE historical accounts of the Brahui principality in Jhalawan (c. 1470 CE during the Arghun era), noting its extension through Jhalawan to Wadh.
b_wad.etymology_analysis: Modern Wadh in Balochistan, Pakistan. Unattested in early Islamic or pre-Islamic written sources; first appears in historical records of the 15th century CE.

b_budin.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (Ahsan al-Taqasim fi Ma'rifat al-Aqalim, c. 985 CE), describing Qusdar as divided into two quarters on opposite sides of a dry riverbed, with the merchant quarter called Budin.
b_budin.etymology_analysis: Recorded by al-Muqaddasi in c. 985 CE as the commercial quarter of Qusdar across the dry riverbed from the ruler's palace and citadel, frequented by merchants from Khurasan. No written attestation exists prior to 867 CE.

b_gajor.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_gajor.etymology_analysis: Modern Gajar (Gajor) in Awaran/Mashkai, Balochistan, Pakistan. While the nearby prehistoric mound of Gajar Damb dates to the Bronze Age (3500-1800 BCE), the name Gajor/Gajar has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_qandabil.first_mention_attestation: 660 CE Rashidun military expedition under al-Harith ibn Murra al-Abdi, who marched from Makran northward to Qandabil (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, and al-Tabari).
b_qandabil.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qandabil (modern Gandava in Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan), the chief town of the Budha/Budahah district in early Islamic sources. Attested from the 7th-century CE Arab conquests (660 CE) and later 10th-century CE geographers.

b_qiqan.first_mention_attestation: 660-663 CE Rashidun/Umayyad campaigns in northeastern Balochistan under al-Harith ibn Murra al-Abdi (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, and subsequent 8th-century CE accounts of the Zutt in Qiqan).

morphemes.translation: highland town and district (identified with modern Kalat/Nal)

b_qiqan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qiqan (also Kikan, Qayqan, and Kizkanan), a strategic highland settlement in Turan (modern Kalat or Nal in Balochistan) inhabited by Zutt tribes and attested in early Islamic conquest narratives from 660-663 CE.

b_bost.first_mention_attestation: 31 AH / 652 CE Arab conquest of Sistan and Bost under Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 394, and Encyclopaedia Iranica).

morphemes.translation: historical fortress city at the Helmand-Arghandab confluence

b_bost.etymology_analysis: Persian Bost (Arabic Bust, modern Qala-e-Bost / Lashkargah in Helmand, Afghanistan). An ancient strategic fortress at the confluence of the Helmand and Arghandab rivers, firmly attested in written accounts of the 652 CE Arab conquest of Sistan.

b_delaram.first_mention_attestation: August 1720 CE Battle of Dilaram between Mahmud Hotak and Asadullah Khan Abdali, recorded in 18th-century CE Afghan and Persian chronicles.
b_delaram.etymology_analysis: New Persian compound Delaram ('heart's ease / restful'), a town in northern Nimruz Province, Afghanistan. Unattested in early Islamic or pre-Islamic sources <= 867 CE.

b_galikan.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Hawqal (Kitab Surat al-Ard, c. 978 CE), describing Az-Zalikan (also spelt Salakan or Jalikan) as a weavers' town one march from Bust.
b_galikan.etymology_analysis: Corresponding to medieval Az-Zalikan / Jalikan (Galikan), a fertile weaving town one day's march from Bust first attested in Ibn Hawqal (c. 978 CE). No written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_al_muaskar.first_mention_attestation: al-Muqaddasi (Ahsan al-Taqasim, c. 985 CE), describing al-'Askar ('the Camp'), the Ghaznavid royal military cantonment half a league from Bust (modern Lashkari Bazar).
b_al_muaskar.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Mu'askar ('the military camp'), referring to the Ghaznavid winter military capital and palace complex of al-'Askar / Lashkari Bazar established near Bost in the late 10th century CE.

b_ribat-i-kish.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_ribat-i-kish.etymology_analysis: Persian-Arabic compound Ribat-i Kish ('caravanserai/waystation of Kish'). No documented written attestation <= 867 CE exists for this ribat.

b_farah.first_mention_attestation: Classical Greek and Parthian sources: Phrada (330 BCE, capital of Drangiana, preserved in Stephanus of Byzantium) and Alexandria Prophthasia (Pliny, Strabo), followed by Phra in Isidore of Charax's Parthian Stations (1st century CE) and Farah in 7th-century CE Islamic conquest accounts (651 CE).
b_farah.etymology_analysis: New Persian Farah (early Islamic Farah), continuing Parthian Phra and Achaemenid/Hellenistic Phrada, demonstrating continuous toponymic survival from the first millennium BCE.

b_juwain.first_mention_attestation: Early 9th-century CE accounts of the Kharijite leader Hamza ibn Adharak (d. 828 CE) and his conflicts with Harun al-Rashid's governors in Sistan (recorded in Tarikh-i Sistan and Ibn al-Athir), as well as Ya'qub al-Saffar's 865 CE campaign.

morphemes.translation: fortress town in northern Sistan (modern Lash-e Jovayn)

b_juwain.etymology_analysis: Arabicized Juwain (Persian Jovayn/Govayn, from Middle Persian *Gawen, possibly the Gabene polis of Isidore of Charax). Well attested as a Kharijite stronghold in northern Sistan from c. 800 CE onward.

b_uq.first_mention_attestation: 251 AH / 865 CE campaign of Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar against the Kharijites around Joveyn and Uq in northern Sistan, where he defeated and killed their leader Ammar ibn Yasir (recorded in Tarikh-i Sistan and Encyclopaedia Iranica).
b_uq.etymology_analysis: Medieval town of Uq (Oq) in northern Sistan near Juwain and Farah, attested in the Tarikh-i Sistan for events of 865 CE during Ya'qub al-Saffar's suppression of local Kharijites.

b_masau.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.

morphemes.translation: village name in Pusht Rod, Farah

b_masau.etymology_analysis: Modern village of Masaw (Masau) in Pusht Rod District, Farah Province, Afghanistan. No documented written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_nih.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arab geographers (al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE), describing Nih as a strongly fortified clay-built town on the Kuhistan-Sistan frontier watered by qanats.
b_nih.etymology_analysis: Persian Nih (modern Nehbandan in South Khorasan, Iran). Although the Nehbandan citadel has Parthian-era archaeological remains and later medieval authors (Yaqut, Mustawfi) attributed its founding to Ardashir I, the earliest documented written attestation of Nih is in 10th-century CE Arab geographers.

b_bandan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_bandan.etymology_analysis: Modern village of Bandan in Nehbandan County, South Khorasan, Iran. Derived from Persian band ('dam, embankment') + plural/toponymic suffix -an. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_doroh.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Nizari Ismaili and Quhistan historical sources (11th-13th centuries CE, e.g., Juzjani's Tabaqat-i Nasiri and Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub), recording Qal'eh-ye Duruh (Dara/Darah) on the Quhistan-Sistan border.
b_doroh.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian Duruh (modern Doreh in Sarbisheh County, South Khorasan, Iran), a fortified mountain settlement on the Quhistan-Sistan frontier prominent during the Nizari Ismaili period (11th-13th centuries CE). Unattested <= 867 CE.

b_khoshk-rud.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_khoshk-rud.etymology_analysis: New Persian hydronym Khoshk-Rud ('Dry River'), referring to a seasonal or dry watercourse in the Sistan basin. No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_rudbar.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Arab conquest of Sistan (c. 661 CE, recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, pp. 393-395), mentioning ar-Rudhbar of Sijistan along the Helmand River.
b_rudbar.etymology_analysis: Persian Rudbar ('riverbank / riverside'), denoting the fertile riverine stretch of the lower Helmand River in Sistan. Attested as ar-Rudhbar in al-Baladhuri's account of the 7th-century CE Muslim conquest.

b_kish-rudbar.first_mention_attestation: 661 CE campaign of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura in Sistan, conquering the region between Zarang and Kisht/Kishsh near ar-Rudhbar (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, pp. 393-395).
b_kish-rudbar.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement of Kishsh/Kisht near ar-Rudhbar on the Helmand River, attested in al-Baladhuri's account of the 661 CE Arab campaign in Sistan.

b_mofd_afdzalkhan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_mofd_afdzalkhan.eponym_details: Afzal Khan (Afdzalkhan) — post-867 CE — Settlement/locality named after a post-867 CE figure bearing the Arabic-Islamic personal name Afzal and the Turco-Mongol/Afghan title Khan.
b_mofd_afdzalkhan.etymology_analysis: Toponym incorporating the post-867 CE personal name and title Afzal Khan (combining Arabic Afzal with the Turco-Mongol/Afghan title Khan), unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_khannesin.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_khannesin.etymology_analysis: Persian compound Khan-neshin ('seat/residence of the Khan'), modern Khanashin in Reg District, Helmand, Afghanistan. Contains the post-867 CE title Khan and has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_landay.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_landay.etymology_analysis: Pashto toponym Landay ('short'), a modern town in Helmand Province, Afghanistan. No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_zaranj.first_mention_attestation: c. 520 BCE Behistun Inscription of Darius I (Old Persian Zranka), classical Greek sources (Zarangiane/Drangiana), and 651-652 CE Arab conquest accounts (Zaranj/Zarang).
b_zaranj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized Zaranj from Middle Persian Zarang and Old Persian Zranka (likely connected to *drayah-, 'sea/lake', referring to the Hamun/Zarah basin). Capital of Sistan from antiquity through the Saffarid era.

b_ram_shahristan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Arab geographers (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE; Ibn Hawqal, c. 978 CE), describing the already-ruined former pre-Islamic capital of Sistan known as Ram Shahristan or Abrashahriyar.
b_ram_shahristan.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Ram Shahristan ('city of peace/joy', also called Abrashahriyar), the ancient/Sasanian capital of Sistan abandoned after a Helmand canal dam burst. Although archaeologically occupied from the 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE, its earliest documented written attestation is in 10th-century CE Arab geographers.

b_qarnin.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, c. 864 CE), mentioning al-Qarnin/Karnin in Sistan (also famous as the birthplace of Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar in 840 CE).

morphemes.translation: town in Sistan between Zaranj and Bost

b_qarnin.etymology_analysis: Medieval town of Qarnin (Karnin) in Sistan, east of Zaranj and west of Bost, birthplace of the Saffarid founder Ya'qub ibn al-Layth (840 CE) and explicitly attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 864 CE).

b_khawaj.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found in available historical sources.
b_khawaj.etymology_analysis: Derived from New Persian khwaja ('master, lord'), likely associated with Kuh-e Khwajeh or a local shrine/settlement in Sistan. No documented written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_karkuya.first_mention_attestation: 651 CE Arab conquest of Sakastan under Rabi ibn Ziyad al-Harithi, who secured the submission of the fortress of Karkuya and its famous Zoroastrian fire temple (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Tarikh-i Sistan, and Encyclopaedia Iranica).

morphemes.translation: fortress and Zoroastrian fire-temple town north of Zaranj

b_karkuya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Karkuya (Karkuyeh) north of Zaranj in Sistan, renowned for its Sasanian Zoroastrian fire temple (Mainyo Karko), attested from the 651 CE Arab conquest of Sakastan.
